web-api-1.pitch: ASP.NET Web API is my go-to for building HTTP/JSON services in .NET.
web-api-1.definition: It is a .NET framework for building HTTP-based RESTful services. It maps HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) directly to controller action methods and returns data (usually JSON) instead of HTML, so any client - browsers, mobile apps, or other services - can consume it over plain HTTP. It ships with built-in routing, model binding, validation and content negotiation, and ASP.NET Core Web API is the modern, cross-platform, high-performance version on .NET 5+.

diagram.title: ASP.NET Web API request flow
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Client] -->|HTTP| B[Routing]
  B --> C[Controller / Action]
  C --> D[(Database)]
  C -->|JSON| A

web-api-1.how: Routing matches URL + verb -> model binding fills params -> filters (auth) -> action runs -> formatter returns JSON. Runs on the middleware pipeline with built-in DI.
web-api-1.when: REST back ends, microservices, SPA and mobile APIs.

code.snippet:
[ApiController]
[Route("api/products")]
public class ProductsController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("{id}")]                       // GET api/products/5
    public ActionResult<Product> Get(int id) =>
        _svc.Find(id) is { } p ? Ok(p) : NotFound();  // 200 + JSON, or 404
}
code.note: [HttpGet] maps verb + URL to the method; Ok/NotFound set the status and serialize JSON.

web-api-1.realWorld: At a fintech, one ASP.NET Core API served a React dashboard and an iOS app via versioned /v1 endpoints + JWT; async + caching cut p95 latency ~40%.

web-api-2.pitch: These are three related ASP.NET stacks - data services, web pages, and the modern unified one.
web-api-2.definition: ASP.NET Web API builds HTTP services that return data (JSON/XML); ASP.NET MVC builds web apps that render HTML views for browsers; both are .NET Framework only. ASP.NET Core Web API is the modern, cross-platform, high-performance successor that merges MVC and Web API into a single framework on .NET 5+. For any new work you use ASP.NET Core; the other two mainly matter for legacy apps.
web-api-2.when: Choose ASP.NET Core Web API for new APIs; MVC when the server renders pages.
keyPoints: Web API: returns data (JSON) for REST
MVC: returns HTML views for browsers
Use Core for all new development

web-api-3.pitch: Web API is REST-first and lightweight; WCF is protocol-flexible but heavy.
web-api-3.definition: ASP.NET Web API is a lightweight framework for building RESTful services over HTTP using simple verbs and JSON. WCF is an older, heavier framework for services across many protocols (HTTP, TCP, named pipes, MSMQ) using SOAP, contracts and bindings. Web API suits the open web and mobile; WCF suits enterprise/intranet scenarios needing non-HTTP transports or WS-* standards.

web-api-4.pitch: Pick Web API for open HTTP/REST; pick WCF only for advanced or non-HTTP needs.
web-api-4.definition: The choice comes down to transport and client needs. ASP.NET Web API is the right call for HTTP/REST services consumed by browsers, mobile apps and other services, with plain JSON and minimal setup. WCF only wins when you specifically need non-HTTP transports (TCP, named pipes, MSMQ), SOAP/WS-* standards, or distributed transactions - otherwise Web API is simpler and more web-friendly.
web-api-4.when: Public REST APIs, SPA/mobile back ends, microservices, simple HTTP/JSON.
web-api-4.whenNot: Need TCP/named pipes/MSMQ, SOAP/WS-*, or distributed transactions.

web-api-5.pitch: The lifecycle is the ordered path a request takes from arrival to response.
web-api-5.definition: When a request arrives it flows through a fixed pipeline: hosting and middleware, then routing, controller and action selection, model binding, filters, the action method, result formatting, and finally the HTTP response. Each stage is an extension point, so cross-cutting concerns like auth, logging and error handling plug in cleanly. Knowing this order is what lets you debug exactly where a request succeeds or fails.

diagram.title: Web API request lifecycle
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Request] --> B[Middleware]
  B --> C[Routing]
  C --> D[Action Select]
  D --> E[Model Binding]
  E --> F[Filters]
  F --> G[Action]
  G --> H[Formatter]
  H --> I[Response]

steps: Hosting and middleware receive the request
Action executes and returns a result

web-api-6.pitch: Routing maps a URL and verb to the right controller action.
web-api-6.definition: Routing is the stage that decides which controller and action handle a request. It compares the incoming URL and HTTP verb against registered route templates - either attribute routes on the methods (e.g. [HttpGet("products/{id}")]) or convention-based templates - then picks the matching action and extracts route values. If two routes match equally it errors as ambiguous; if none match it returns 404.

diagram.title: Request routing
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[URL + Verb] --> B[Match Template]
  B --> C[Controller]
  C --> D[Action]
  D --> E[Bind Values]

steps: Read the request path and HTTP verb
Compare them to registered route templates
Select the matching controller and action
Hand off to model binding (or 404 if no match)

web-api-7.pitch: HTTP verbs express what a request intends to do to a resource.
web-api-7.definition: HTTP verbs are the action words of REST: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces a whole resource, PATCH updates part of it, DELETE removes it, HEAD returns headers only, and OPTIONS reports the allowed methods. GET and PUT are idempotent and GET is safe, which helps caching and safe retries. Using the correct verb is what makes an API predictable and properly RESTful.
web-api-7.when: GET to fetch, POST to create, PUT/PATCH to update, DELETE to remove.
keyPoints: PUT: replace fully / PATCH: update part
HEAD: headers only / OPTIONS: allowed methods

web-api-8.pitch: Status codes tell the client the outcome of a request.
web-api-8.definition: HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers grouped by meaning: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. They let any client understand a result without custom logic and drive correct caching, retries and error handling. Returning the right code (not 200 for everything) is what keeps an API honest and easy to monitor.

web-api-9.pitch: REST is a stateless, resource-based style for HTTP APIs.
web-api-9.definition: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for networked APIs where everything is a resource identified by a URL and manipulated with standard HTTP verbs and representations like JSON. Its principles are client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, a uniform interface, a layered system, and resource-based design. These constraints are what make REST simple, scalable and widely interoperable.

diagram.title: REST interaction
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] -->|GET /products| S[Server]
  S -->|200 + JSON| C
  C -->|POST /products| S
  S -->|201 Created| C

web-api-10.pitch: CORS is the browser rule that lets one origin safely call another.
web-api-10.definition: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that uses HTTP headers to let a server declare which other origins may call it, relaxing the same-origin policy in a controlled way. For non-simple requests the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight first; the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-* headers, and only then does the browser allow the real request. It is enforced by browsers, so it protects users - it is not a server-side firewall.

diagram.title: CORS preflight
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  B[Browser] -->|OPTIONS| S[Server]
  S -->|Allow-Origin/Methods| B
  B -->|Actual request| S
  S -->|Response| B

steps: Browser app on origin A calls API on origin B
If allowed, browser sends the real request
Otherwise the browser blocks the response

web-api-11.pitch: Enable CORS by registering a policy and applying it in the pipeline.
web-api-11.definition: In ASP.NET Core you enable CORS by registering a named policy with AddCors and applying it with UseCors in the middleware pipeline, specifying the allowed origins, methods and headers. The policy can be applied globally or per endpoint with [EnableCors]. Order matters - UseCors must sit before MapControllers, and AllowAnyOrigin cannot be combined with credentials.
steps: Call builder.Services.AddCors with a named policy

code.note: WithOrigins whitelists the front-end; UseCors must run before the endpoints.

web-api-12.pitch: Parameter binding fills action parameters from the request.
web-api-12.definition: Parameter binding is how Web API populates an action method's parameters from the incoming request. By default simple types (int, string) bind from the route or query string, while complex types bind from the request body. You can override the source with attributes like [FromQuery], [FromRoute], [FromBody] or [FromHeader], and only one [FromBody] parameter is allowed per action.
keyPoints: Complex types bind from the body

web-api-13.pitch: Model binding builds objects; parameter binding is the wider concept.
web-api-13.definition: Model binding is the process that builds complex objects from multiple request sources - body, route, query, form, headers - and validates them into ModelState. Parameter binding is the broader umbrella that also covers mapping simple scalar values to parameters. In short, model binding is the complex-type part of parameter binding, and [From*] attributes let you control the source for both.

web-api-14.pitch: Content negotiation picks the response format the client asked for.
web-api-14.definition: Content negotiation is the process where the API and client agree on a response format such as JSON or XML, based on the request's Accept header and the formatters the server supports. The server selects the best matching formatter, serializes the result and sets the Content-Type; if nothing matches it returns 406 Not Acceptable. This lets a single endpoint serve multiple media types.
steps: It serializes the response and sets Content-Type

web-api-15.pitch: Formatters serialize objects out and deserialize the body in.
web-api-15.definition: Media-type formatters are the components that turn a .NET object into a wire format (like JSON) on the way out and parse the request body into a .NET object on the way in. Content negotiation picks the output formatter from the Accept header, while the Content-Type picks the input formatter. They are pluggable, so you can register custom formatters for new media types in MVC options.
web-api-15.how: Request: the formatter matching Content-Type reads the body into an object. Response: content negotiation picks a formatter for the Accept header, which serializes the result and sets Content-Type.

web-api-16.pitch: JSON is the light default; XML is verbose but enterprise-friendly.
web-api-16.definition: JSON and XML formatters serialize responses into those formats. JSON is compact, fast and native to JavaScript clients, so it is the default in ASP.NET Core; XML is more verbose but supports schemas and namespaces and is still used by some enterprise clients. You can support both and let content negotiation choose, and you set the default via formatter configuration or [Produces].
web-api-16.how: JSON is default; add XML with AddControllers().AddXmlSerializerFormatters(). Force a format with [Produces("application/json")]; otherwise content negotiation and formatter order decide.

web-api-17.pitch: Filters run code at set points to handle cross-cutting concerns.
web-api-17.definition: Filters let you run logic at specific points in the pipeline without repeating it in every action. Authentication filters establish who the caller is, authorization filters decide whether they may proceed, action filters run before/after the action (logging, validation), and exception filters catch unhandled errors and shape the response. They can be applied globally, per controller, or per action.

web-api-18.definition: The [Authorize] attribute marks a controller or action as requiring an authenticated user before it runs, and can additionally demand roles or policies. It checks the ClaimsPrincipal set by authentication: plain [Authorize] needs any authenticated user, while [Authorize(Roles="Admin")] or [Authorize(Policy="...")] add finer checks. Failing returns 401 (not authenticated) or 403 (not allowed); [AllowAnonymous] opens specific endpoints.

code.note: [Authorize] gates the endpoint by identity/role; [AllowAnonymous] re-opens it.

web-api-19.pitch: Basic Auth sends Base64 username:password on every request.
web-api-19.definition: Basic Authentication is the simplest HTTP auth scheme: the client sends the username and password, Base64-encoded, in the Authorization header on every request. It is trivial to implement and universally supported, but Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so the credentials are only safe over HTTPS and there is no expiry or revocation without changing the password. It is fine for quick internal tools, not for public APIs.

web-api-20.pitch: JWT auth issues a signed token the client sends on each call.
web-api-20.definition: JWT bearer authentication issues a signed JSON Web Token after the user logs in; the client then sends it in the Authorization: Bearer header on every request, and the API validates the signature, expiry and claims without storing any session. Because the token is self-contained and stateless, it scales well and works across services - the trade-off is that tokens cannot easily be revoked before they expire.

diagram.title: JWT flow
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[Client] -->|Login| A[Auth Server]
  A -->|Signed JWT| U
  U -->|Bearer JWT| P[API]
  P -->|Validate| P
  P -->|200 + data| U

steps: Auth server returns a signed JWT

web-api-21.pitch: OAuth is the protocol to get a token; JWT is the token's format.
web-api-21.definition: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that defines how a client obtains an access token from an authorization server through flows like authorization code or client credentials. JWT is simply a compact, signed token format. They are complementary, not competing: OAuth answers 'how do I get and use a token', and that access token is very often a JWT.

web-api-22.pitch: Versioning lets an API change without breaking existing clients.
web-api-22.definition: API versioning lets you evolve an API without breaking the clients you do not control. The common approaches are URL path (/v1/), query string (?api-version=1), header, and media-type versioning. I recommend URL-path versioning because it is explicit, easy to test, cache and document, and clients can see exactly which version they call; header or media-type versioning is a fine alternative when URLs must stay clean.
web-api-22.why: Public APIs have clients you do not control, so a breaking change without a new version breaks them; versioning lets clients upgrade on their own schedule.
bestPractices: Prefer URL-path versioning - explicit and cacheable
Deprecate old versions with a clear timeline

web-api-23.pitch: Global handling turns any error into one consistent response.
web-api-23.definition: Exception handling converts errors into proper HTTP responses, and global exception handling does it in one place so every unhandled error returns a consistent, safe payload. You add exception-handling middleware (or UseExceptionHandler / IExceptionHandler) early in the pipeline; it catches the error, logs it with context, maps it to a status code, and returns a standard ProblemDetails body without leaking internals.
steps: Add exception middleware early in the pipeline
Log it with context and a correlation id
Map it to a status code (400/404/500)

code.note: One middleware catches every unhandled error and returns a safe JSON body.

web-api-24.pitch: Filters catch MVC errors; middleware catches everything.
web-api-24.definition: Exception filters handle errors thrown inside the MVC/controller layer and have access to the action context, so they are good for controller-specific handling. Global exception middleware sits earlier in the pipeline and catches errors from anywhere, including other middleware. They are often combined: filters for fine-grained cases, middleware as the catch-all backstop.

web-api-25.pitch: DI hands a class its dependencies instead of newing them up.
web-api-25.definition: Dependency Injection is a pattern where a class receives its dependencies from an external container instead of constructing them itself, and ASP.NET Core has DI built in and uses it everywhere. You register services with a lifetime (singleton, scoped, transient) and the framework injects them through constructors. This gives loose coupling, easy testing with mocks, and managed object lifetimes - it is the backbone of clean ASP.NET Core apps.
web-api-25.why: It removes hard-coded 'new' calls, so you can swap real vs mock implementations, test in isolation, and let the framework manage lifetimes.

code.note: Register the interface once; the container injects it wherever it is needed.

web-api-26.pitch: Secure an API with layered defenses on every endpoint.
web-api-26.definition: You secure a Web API by applying layered defenses: parameterize all queries to stop SQL injection, validate and encode output plus set a CSP to stop XSS, and use anti-forgery tokens or bearer tokens with SameSite cookies to stop CSRF. On top of that, enforce HTTPS, authentication and authorization, rate limiting, least-privilege DB accounts, and keep dependencies patched. Security must be consistent on every endpoint, not bolted on.
keyPoints: XSS: validate + encode output, set CSP
bestPractices: Never concatenate user input into SQL
Treat all input as untrusted - validate it
Keep secrets out of code (use a vault)

web-api-27.pitch: Speed up an API by cutting work, payload and blocking.
web-api-27.definition: You improve Web API performance by reducing repeated work, shrinking payloads, and freeing threads. The main levers are caching (response and data), response compression, asynchronous I/O with async/await, pagination and lean payloads, and query/connection optimization. The golden rule is to measure with profiling before optimizing, so you fix the real bottleneck rather than guessing.
keyPoints: Cache hot data + set cache headers
Page, filter, project only needed fields
Add DB indexes, reuse pooled connections
bestPractices: Cache with a clear invalidation strategy

web-api-28.pitch: Swagger documents the API; Postman exercises it.
web-api-28.definition: You document and test Web APIs with Swagger/OpenAPI and Postman. Swashbuckle generates an OpenAPI spec and an interactive Swagger UI straight from your controllers and XML comments, so the docs stay current and clients can be generated. Postman lets you build, save and automate requests in collections, with environment variables and test scripts that can run in CI via Newman.
steps: Add Swashbuckle to generate swagger.json + UI
Annotate models, responses and XML comments
Build a Postman collection per API
Use env variables for base URLs and tokens
Run collections in CI with Newman

web-api-29.pitch: Observability = structured logs, metrics, and correlation IDs.
web-api-29.definition: You monitor and troubleshoot production APIs with structured logging, centralized aggregation, metrics and health checks, and correlation IDs that tie all logs of a single request together across services. A logging framework (ILogger/Serilog) writes JSON to a sink like Seq, ELK or Application Insights; a correlation id flows through every log and downstream call; and distributed tracing follows a request end to end. This is what turns a vague 'it is slow' into a precise root cause.
keyPoints: Structured JSON logs to a central sink
Correlation id per request, on every log
Never log secrets; control log volume
bestPractices: Always attach a correlation id to logs
Log enough context, not sensitive data
Alert on error rate and latency, not just CPU

web-api-30.pitch: Design it stateless, scalable, secured and automated end to end.
web-api-30.definition: A high-traffic Web API is designed as stateless, horizontally scalable services behind a load balancer and API gateway, with token-based auth, URL versioning, centralized error handling, caching and async I/O, all shipped through an automated pipeline. Statelessness plus load balancing lets you scale out, caching and a CDN absorb read traffic, and CI/CD with health checks enables safe, frequent releases. The trade-off is more moving parts to operate and monitor.

diagram.title: High-traffic API architecture
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Clients] --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> G[API Gateway / Auth]
  G --> S1[API Instance]
  G --> S2[API Instance]
  S1 --> Cache[(Cache)]
  S1 --> DB[(Database)]
  S2 --> Cache
  S2 --> DB

keyPoints: Stateless services behind LB + API gateway
JWT/OAuth bearer auth at the edge
Caching/CDN, async I/O, paging, tuned queries
Resilience: retries, rate limit, circuit breaker
